raw_response:
I'm 55, been on this land since I was twenty when I married into this village. Never went to school — my parents said girls didn't need it, and anyway there was work to do. But thirty-five years of farming teaches you things no book can. I know every patch of my 10 mu like the back of my hand.

It's just me and my husband now. He's 58, works part-time at a construction site in the county town — comes back for the busy seasons, wheat harvest and cotton picking. Our son is in Shijiazhuang working in a warehouse. So most days it's me out there alone. I have to be careful with money and with my body. I can't afford to get hurt or to waste a single yuan.

I split my land two ways. About 6 and a half mu I do wheat then maize, same as most folks around here. The other 3 and a half mu, almost 4, I grow cotton. I've kept that cotton plot for fifteen years. It's hard work, especially the picking, but it's the only way we get real cash.

**Winter wheat** — I planted it last October right after the National Day holiday. I bought new seed this year because my saved seed was looking weak and spotty, about 40 jin per mu. Before planting I put down base fertilizer, half a bag of that compound fertilizer with the three numbers on it. Now it's spring, the wheat is waking up. I'll spread urea soon when the weather warms — about 50 jin per mu. I did 40 jin last year and my wheat was yellower than Wang's from the east end of the village, so I'm not skimping this time. Better to spend a bit more than to lose half the crop. I'll water three times: green-up, jointing, and grain-filling. The well is right there but the electricity bill adds up. I'll spray herbicide once, and if I see aphids I'll spray insecticide too.

**Summer maize** — that goes in right after we cut the wheat in early June. The window is tight, sometimes only five or six days. I hire the combine for wheat harvest, then I rush to get the rotary tiller through and plant the maize. I buy hybrid seed, about 3 jin per mu. I put compound fertilizer and some urea in the holes at planting. When the maize is knee-high, I topdress with more urea. I'll irrigate twice if the rain doesn't come — usually at jointing and when the ears are filling. My husband will be back to help with this, thank goodness.

**Cotton** — I plant in late April. I plow that field first when the soil warms up and dries out a bit. Cotton seed is cheap, I use about 3 to 4 jin per mu. Base fertilizer goes in before planting — some compound fertilizer. Then when the yellow flowers come in July, I spread urea again. Cotton needs spraying for bollworm, I usually do three or four sprays. Water it twice: once after planting to settle it, and again at flowering. The worst part is picking. Me and my husband pick what we can, but we have to hire women from the village. They get paid by the jin. Last year it was almost 1 yuan per jin. It's expensive, but if you don't pick on time the cotton gets dirty and the buyer pays less.

Money is tight. Fertilizer prices went up again this year. I thought about using less on the maize, but my sister's family tried that two years ago and their yield dropped by half when the summer turned dry. I'd rather borrow 500 yuan from my cousin than risk it. We need the wheat for our own flour and some feed, the maize sells to the grain dealer who drives his truck by the village road, and the cotton is what pays for my husband's medicine and the house repairs. If the weather is fair and the well doesn't run dry, we should be alright.
